notes.front: What is Azure Resource Manager (ARM)?
notes.back: Azure's deployment and management service: a management layer for creating, updating and deleting resources in your Azure account.
notes.explanation: After deployment you use its management features, such as access control, locks and tags, to secure and organise resources.
notes.example: Like a building's facilities office: it handles every request to add, alter or remove a room, and keeps the keys and labels afterwards.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Resource Manager?”
notes.evidence: Azure Resource Manager is the deployment and management service for Azure. It provides a management layer that helps you to create, update, and delete resources in your Azure account. You use management features like access control, locks, and tags to secure and organize your resources after deployment.

notes.front: What is a resource group?
notes.back: A container that holds related resources for an Azure solution: the resources you want to manage as a group.
notes.explanation: You decide which resources belong together, based on what makes most sense for your organisation.
notes.example: Like a project folder: a shop's web app, its database and its network sit in one folder so they can be handled together.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Terminology”
notes.evidence: resource group - A container that holds related resources for an Azure solution. The resource group includes those resources that you want to manage as a group. You decide which resources belong in a resource group based on what makes the most sense for your organization.

notes.front: What is a management group?
notes.back: A governance scope above subscriptions; governance conditions applied to it cascade by inheritance to every subscription inside.
notes.explanation: It gives organisations with many subscriptions an efficient way to manage access, policies and compliance across them.
notes.example: Like a division that holds several team budgets: a spending rule set for the division applies to every team under it.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What are Azure management groups?”
notes.evidence: Management groups provide a governance scope above subscriptions. When you organize subscriptions into management groups, the governance conditions that you apply cascade by inheritance to all associated subscriptions.

notes.front: What is the root management group?
notes.back: The single top-level management group in each directory, into which all management groups and subscriptions fold.
notes.explanation: It is where global policies and Azure role assignments can be applied at directory level.
notes.example: Like the trunk of a tree: every branch and leaf, however far out, joins it.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Root management group for each directory”
notes.evidence: Each directory has a single top-level management group called the root management group. The root management group is built into the hierarchy to have all management groups and subscriptions fold up to it. The root management group allows for the application of global policies and Azure role assignments at the directory level.

notes.front: What is an Azure landing zone?
notes.back: A proven, flexible architecture for governing, securing and scaling a multi-subscription Azure environment.
notes.explanation: It is designed in the Ready phase of Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework to meet the organisation's own requirements.
notes.example: Like the roads, drains and power laid on a building site before any houses go up.
notes.source: What is an Azure landing zone? (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “What is an Azure landing zone?”
notes.evidence: The Ready phase of the Cloud Adoption Framework helps you design your Azure landing zone to meet your organization's requirements. An Azure landing zone is a proven and flexible architecture for governing, securing, and scaling a multi-subscription Azure environment.

notes.front: What are resource tags?
notes.back: Metadata elements applied to Azure resources: key-value pairs that help identify resources by settings relevant to your organisation.
notes.explanation: Each tag is a name and a value you choose, so the labels reflect your own organisation's settings.
notes.example: Like luggage labels: Owner = Finance tells anyone which team a database belongs to.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy”
notes.evidence: Tags are metadata elements that you apply to your Azure resources. They are key-value pairs that help you identify resources based on settings that are relevant to your organization.

notes.front: What are resource locks?
notes.back: Locks on a subscription, resource group or resource that protect it from accidental deletion or modification.
notes.explanation: A lock overrides any user permissions, so it protects the item whatever access a user has.
notes.example: Like a padlock on a filing cabinet that even the office manager must remove before the cabinet can be thrown away.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: As an administrator, you can lock an Azure subscription, resource group, or resource to protect them from accidental user deletions and modifications. The lock overrides any user permissions.

notes.front: What is Azure Policy?
notes.back: A service that helps enforce organisational standards and assess compliance at scale.
notes.explanation: Its compliance dashboard gives an aggregated view of the environment, with drill-down to each resource and each policy.
notes.example: Like building regulations with an inspector: the rules are written once, and every new or existing building is checked against them.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: This overview describes how Azure Policy helps to enforce organizational standards and to assess compliance at-scale. Through its compliance dashboard, it provides an aggregated view to evaluate the overall state of the environment, with the ability to drill down to the per-resource, per-policy granularity.

notes.front: What is a policy definition in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A business rule against which Azure Policy compares the properties of resources.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions by checking their properties against these rules.
notes.example: Like one rule in a club's handbook, such as 'guests must sign in', together with what happens when it is broken.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Overview”
notes.evidence: Azure Policy evaluates resources and actions in Azure by comparing the properties of those resources to business rules. These business rules, described in JSON format, are known as policy definitions.

notes.front: What is an initiative definition in Azure Policy?
notes.back: A collection of policy definitions tailored towards one overarching goal, handled as a single item.
notes.explanation: Grouping the policies simplifies managing and assigning them.
notes.example: Like a fire-safety checklist: many separate rules gathered under the one goal of passing inspection.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Initiative definition”
notes.evidence: An initiative definition is a collection of policy definitions that are tailored toward achieving a singular overarching goal. Initiative definitions simplify managing and assigning policy definitions. They simplify by grouping a set of policies as one single item.

notes.front: What is a policy assignment?
notes.back: A policy definition or initiative assigned to a specific scope, anywhere from a management group down to a single resource.
notes.explanation: The scope covers all the resources, resource groups, subscriptions or management groups the definition is assigned to.
notes.example: Like pinning a rule to one office's noticeboard, so it applies to that office and everything in it.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Assignments”
notes.evidence: An assignment is a policy definition or initiative that was assigned to a specific scope. This scope could range from a management group to an individual resource. The term scope refers to all the resources, resource groups, subscriptions, or management groups that the definition is assigned to.

notes.front: What is Azure Blueprints?
notes.back: A preview service for defining a repeatable set of Azure resources that follows an organisation's standards, patterns and requirements.
notes.explanation: Development teams can then build new environments quickly, trusting that they stay within organisational compliance.
notes.example: Like a standard house design a builder can put up again and again, each copy meeting the same building code.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Blueprints (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Blueprints (Preview)?”
notes.evidence: Azure Blueprints enables cloud architects and central information technology groups to define a repeatable set of Azure resources that implements and adheres to an organization's standards, patterns, and requirements. Azure Blueprints makes it possible for development teams to rapidly build and start up new environments with trust they're building within organizational compliance

notes.front: What is Azure Resource Graph?
notes.back: A service that extends Azure Resource Manager with efficient resource exploration, querying at scale across a set of subscriptions.
notes.explanation: Querying at scale is what lets you govern a large environment effectively.
notes.example: Like a search engine over your whole Azure estate, instead of opening each subscription in turn.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Resource Graph (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Resource Graph?”
notes.evidence: Azure Resource Graph is an Azure service designed to extend Azure Resource Management by providing efficient and performant resource exploration. Resource Graph has the ability to query at scale across a given set of subscriptions so that you can effectively govern your environment.

notes.front: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: Microsoft's cloud-native application protection platform: one solution joining several cloud security tools to protect applications throughout their lifecycle.
notes.explanation: It gives a single view of security posture across cloud and on-premises resources, including multicloud and hybrid estates.
notes.example: Like a combined building surveyor and security guard for your cloud, both reporting to one control room.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is cloud security posture management (CSPM) in Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: The core component that checks and improves the security posture of cloud resources.
notes.explanation: How secure a resource is depends on it being configured and deployed properly, so CSPM looks for weaknesses in the set-up and recommends fixes.
notes.example: Like a surveyor who walks round a house pointing out unlocked windows and loose wiring before anyone breaks in.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “Cloud security posture management (CSPM)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cloud workload protection platform (CWPP) in Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: The core component that defends workloads, such as virtual machines, containers and databases, from threats.
notes.explanation: It gives workload-specific advice on security controls and raises alerts when a workload is threatened.
notes.example: Like a guard posted inside each building, rather than a surveyor checking how the building was put together.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “Cloud workload protection platform (CWPP)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: The page where you manage compliance standards and review each standard's controls and the assessments behind them.
notes.explanation: Defender for Cloud keeps assessing resources against compliance controls and shows what is blocking a given certification.
notes.example: Like a school report with one page per subject, each showing which requirements are met and which are not.
notes.source: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Microsoft Learn), “Improve regulatory compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Microsoft Cost Management?
notes.back: A suite of FinOps tools that help organisations analyse, monitor and optimise their Microsoft Cloud costs.
notes.explanation: Anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group or management group can use it.
notes.example: Like a household budgeting app linked to every card the family uses.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Cost Management (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Microsoft Cost Management”
notes.evidence: Microsoft Cost Management is a suite of FinOps tools that help organizations analyze, monitor, and optimize their Microsoft Cloud costs. Cost Management is available to anyone with access to a billing account, subscription, resource group, or management group.

notes.front: What are budgets and cost alerts in Cost Management?
notes.back: A budget sets a cost or forecast amount, and budget alerts notify recipients when cost goes beyond it.
notes.explanation: Budgets are available on every scope Cost Management supports and can be viewed in Cost Analysis.
notes.example: Like a bank text that warns you when this month's card spending passes a limit you set.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Cost Management (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Monitor costs with alerts”
notes.evidence: Budget alerts notify recipients when cost exceeds a predefined cost or forecast amount. Budgets can be visualized in Cost Analysis and are available on every scope supported by Cost Management.

notes.front: What is Privileged Identity Management (PIM)?
notes.back: A Microsoft Entra ID service to manage, control and monitor access to important resources in your organisation.
notes.explanation: The resources it covers are in Microsoft Entra ID, Azure and other Microsoft Online Services such as Microsoft 365.
notes.example: Like a hotel master key kept at reception: staff sign it out only when they need it, and every use is logged.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management? (MicrosoftDocs entra-docs), “Overview”
notes.evidence: Privileged Identity Management (PIM) is a service in Microsoft Entra ID that enables you to manage, control, and monitor access to important resources in your organization. These resources include resources in Microsoft Entra ID, Azure, and other Microsoft Online Services such as Microsoft 365 or Microsoft Intune.

notes.front: What are access reviews in Microsoft Entra ID?
notes.back: A feature for efficiently managing group memberships, access to enterprise applications and role assignments by reviewing user access regularly.
notes.explanation: Regular review makes sure only the right people keep their access.
notes.example: Like a quarterly check of who still holds a key to the office, taking back the keys nobody needs.
notes.source: What are access reviews? (MicrosoftDocs entra-docs), “What are access reviews?”
notes.evidence: Access reviews in Microsoft Entra ID, part of Microsoft Entra, enable organizations to efficiently manage group memberships, access to enterprise applications, and role assignments. User access can be reviewed regularly to make sure only the right people have continued access.

notes.front: What is entitlement management?
notes.back: An identity governance feature that manages identity and access lifecycle at scale.
notes.explanation: It does this by automating access request workflows, access assignments, reviews and expiry.
notes.example: Like an online form for joining a project that goes to an approver and cancels the access when the project ends.
notes.source: What is entitlement management? (MicrosoftDocs entra-docs), “What is entitlement management?”
notes.evidence: Entitlement management is an identity governance feature that enables organizations to manage identity and access lifecycle at scale, by automating access request workflows, access assignments, reviews, and expiration.

notes.front: What is an access package in entitlement management?
notes.back: A bundle of all the resources, with the access, that an identity needs to work on a project or perform a task.
notes.explanation: It can govern access both for internal identities and for identities from outside the organisation.
notes.example: Like a new-starter pack: building pass, laptop login and team chat membership handed over together.
notes.source: What is entitlement management? (MicrosoftDocs entra-docs), “What are access packages and what resources can I manage with them?”
notes.evidence: An access package is a bundle of all the resources with the access an identity needs to work on a project or perform their task. Access packages can be used to govern access for internal identities, and also for identities who originate outside your organization.

notes.front: What is a connected organisation in entitlement management?
notes.back: An external Microsoft Entra directory or domain you have a relationship with, whose identities a policy can allow to request access.
notes.explanation: Naming a partner this way lets its people be specified in an access package policy as allowed to request access.
notes.example: Like putting a supplier on an approved list so that its staff may apply for site passes.
notes.source: What is entitlement management? (MicrosoftDocs entra-docs), “Summary of terminology”
notes.evidence: An external Microsoft Entra directory or domain that you have a relationship with. The identities from a connected organization can be specified in a policy as being allowed to request access.

notes.front: One engineer creates a storage account with a PowerShell script while another creates one in the Azure portal. Which service authenticates and authorises both requests before they reach the storage service?
notes.back: Azure Resource Manager.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Resource Manager
B) Azure Resource Graph
C) Azure Policy
notes.choicesExplained: B: Resource Graph queries and explores resources; it does not receive create requests. C: Azure Policy evaluates requests for compliance but does not authenticate them.
notes.explanation: Every request from any Azure tool goes through the same Resource Manager interface, which is why results and capabilities are consistent across tools.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Consistent management layer”
notes.evidence: When you send a request through any of the Azure APIs, tools, or SDKs, Resource Manager receives the request. It authenticates and authorizes the request before forwarding it to the appropriate Azure service. Because all requests are handled through the same API, you see consistent results and capabilities in all the different tools.

notes.front: Of Azure's four levels of management scope, which one sits directly above subscriptions?
notes.back: Management groups.
notes.explanation: The four levels, from the top, are management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Understand scope”
notes.evidence: Azure provides four levels of management scope: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and resources.

notes.front: Of Azure's four levels of management scope, which one sits between subscriptions and individual resources?
notes.back: Resource groups.
notes.explanation: Resources sit at the lowest level; a resource group gathers them within one subscription.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Understand scope”
notes.evidence: Azure provides four levels of management scope: management groups, subscriptions, resource groups, and resources.

notes.front: You apply a policy at subscription scope. Which resource groups and resources does it reach?
notes.back: All the resource groups and resources in that subscription.
notes.explanation: Lower levels inherit settings from higher ones, so the level you choose decides how widely a setting applies.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Understand scope”
notes.evidence: You apply management settings at any of these levels of scope. The level you select determines how widely the setting is applied. Lower levels inherit settings from higher levels. For example, when you apply a policy to the subscription, the policy is applied to all resource groups and resources in your subscription.

notes.front: A web front end is torn down and redeployed every week, while its customer database is meant to last for years. Should they share one resource group?
notes.back: No. They have different lifecycles, so the database belongs in another resource group.
notes.choices:
A) No, put them in separate resource groups
B) Yes, because they belong to the same application
C) Yes, but add a tag to the database
notes.choicesExplained: B: belonging to one application is not the test; sharing a lifecycle is, and a resource can still connect to resources in other groups. C: a tag does not change the fact that the two are deployed and deleted on different cycles.
notes.explanation: Resources in one group should be deployed, updated and deleted together.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is a resource group?”
notes.evidence: All resources in your resource group should share the same lifecycle. You deploy, update, and delete them together. For example, a server is one resource. If it needs to exist on a different deployment cycle, it should be in another resource group.

notes.front: What happens to the resources in a resource group when you delete the group?
notes.back: They are all deleted too.
notes.explanation: When a solution is finished, deleting its resource group removes everything in it in one step.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is a resource group?”
notes.evidence: Or, when you're finished with the solution, you can delete the resource group and know that all of the resources are deleted.

notes.front: Each resource can exist in {{c1::only one}} resource group, although you can move it to another group.
notes.explanation: You can add a resource to a group, remove it or move it between groups at any time.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is a resource group?”
notes.evidence: Each resource can exist in only one resource group. You can add or remove a resource to a resource group at any time. You can move a resource from one resource group to another group.

notes.front: What does the location you give a resource group determine?
notes.back: Where the metadata about its resources is stored.
notes.explanation: Compliance rules may require that this data be stored in a particular region.
notes.source: What is Azure Resource Manager? (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Which location should I use for my resource group?”
notes.evidence: The resource group stores metadata about resources. When you specify a location for the resource group, you're also specifying where that metadata is stored. For compliance reasons, you might need to ensure that your data is stored in a particular region.

notes.front: What must all the subscriptions within one management group have in common?
notes.back: They must trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant.
notes.explanation: Management groups work whatever type of subscription you have, but not across tenants.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What are Azure management groups?”
notes.evidence: Management groups give you enterprise-grade management at scale, no matter what type of subscriptions you might have. However, all subscriptions within a single management group must trust the same Microsoft Entra tenant.

notes.front: An internal audit team needs read access to 30 subscriptions, and more subscriptions are added every month. What is the simplest design?
notes.back: Place the subscriptions under one management group and make a single role assignment on it.
notes.choices:
A) One role assignment on a management group that holds the subscriptions
B) A scripted role assignment in each subscription
C) A ReadOnly lock on each subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: it works, but every new subscription needs another assignment, which the management group avoids. C: a lock restricts changes for everyone; it grants no access.
notes.explanation: The role assigned at the management group is inherited by all the subscriptions under it, so one assignment replaces many.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hierarchy of management groups and subscriptions”
notes.evidence: By moving multiple subscriptions under a management group, you can create one Azure role assignment on the management group. The role inherits that access to all the subscriptions.

notes.front: A policy limiting virtual machine locations is applied to a management group. Can the owner of a subscription beneath it alter that policy?
notes.back: No. The policy is inherited by the descendant subscriptions, and their owners can't alter it.
notes.explanation: Keeping the policy out of subscription owners' hands is what allows improved governance.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Hierarchy of management groups and subscriptions”
notes.evidence: This policy inherits all the Enterprise Agreement (EA) subscriptions that are descendants of that management group and applies to all VMs under those subscriptions. The resource or subscription owner can't alter this security policy, to allow for improved governance.

notes.front: A design places seven levels of nested management groups between the root management group and the subscriptions. Is it supported?
notes.back: No. A management group tree supports up to six levels of depth, not counting the root or subscription levels.
notes.choices:
A) No, the limit is six levels below the root
B) Yes, there is no depth limit
C) Yes, because the root level is not counted
notes.choicesExplained: B: there is a documented limit of six levels of depth. C: even without the root, seven levels exceed the limit of six.
notes.explanation: The limit counts only the management group levels in between, not the root level or the subscription level.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about management groups”
notes.evidence: A management group tree can support up to six levels of depth. This limit doesn't include the root level or the subscription level.

notes.front: A single directory can support {{c1::10,000}} management groups.
notes.explanation: This is the documented ceiling on management groups in one directory.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about management groups”
notes.evidence: A single directory can support 10,000 management groups.

notes.front: Can one subscription sit under both a Finance management group and a Europe management group at the same time?
notes.back: No. Each management group and subscription can have only one parent.
notes.choices:
A) No, it can have only one parent
B) Yes, a subscription can have up to two parents
C) Yes, if both groups are directly under the root
notes.choicesExplained: B: the documented rule is one parent for each management group and subscription. C: position in the hierarchy does not change the one-parent rule.
notes.explanation: A management group can have many children, but everything sits in a single hierarchy per directory.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about management groups”
notes.evidence: Each management group and subscription can support only one parent. - Each management group can have many children. - All subscriptions and management groups are within a single hierarchy in each directory.

notes.front: What is the root management group's default display name, and what is its ID?
notes.back: Its display name is 'Tenant root group'; its ID is the Microsoft Entra tenant ID.
notes.explanation: The root operates as a management group in its own right, tied to the tenant.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about the root management group”
notes.evidence: By default, the root management group's display name is **Tenant root group**, and it operates itself as a management group. The ID is the same value as the Microsoft Entra tenant ID.

notes.front: Unlike other management groups, the root management group {{c1::can't be moved or deleted}}.
notes.explanation: Every management group and subscription folds up into this one root within the directory.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about the root management group”
notes.evidence: The root management group can't be moved or deleted, unlike other management groups. - All subscriptions and management groups fold up into one root management group within the directory.

notes.front: Who has access to the root management group by default?
notes.back: No one. Only Microsoft Entra Global Administrators can elevate themselves to gain access.
notes.explanation: Once they have access, they can assign any Azure role to other users to manage the group.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about the root management group”
notes.evidence: No one has default access to the root management group. Microsoft Entra Global Administrators are the only users who can elevate themselves to gain access. After they have access to the root management group, they can assign any Azure role to other users to manage the group.

notes.front: Why should user access and policy assignments at the root management group be 'must have' only?
notes.back: Any assignment there applies to all resources within the directory.
notes.explanation: Because of that reach, the documentation asks every customer to weigh the need for each item at this scope.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about the root management group”
notes.evidence: Any assignment of user access or policy on the root management group applies to all resources within the directory. Because of this access level, all customers should evaluate the need to have items defined on this scope. User access and policy assignments should be "must have" only at this scope.

notes.front: A team creates a new subscription, and nobody has configured a default management group. Where does the subscription land in the hierarchy?
notes.back: Under the root management group.
notes.choices:
A) Under the root management group
B) Outside the hierarchy until someone moves it
C) Under the management group of the user who created it
notes.choicesExplained: B: every subscription is part of the directory's single hierarchy. C: placement does not follow the creator; the default is the root.
notes.explanation: New subscriptions default to the root management group when they are created, so anything assigned at the root applies to them.
notes.source: Organize your resources with management groups (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Important facts about the root management group”
notes.evidence: New subscriptions automatically default to the root management group when they're created.

notes.front: By default, who can create new management groups in a Microsoft Entra tenant?
notes.back: Any principal in the tenant, such as a user principal or service principal.
notes.explanation: The landing zone guidance advises enabling Azure RBAC authorisation for management group operations, which overrides this default.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group design considerations”
notes.evidence: Enable Azure role-based access control (RBAC) authorization for management group operations to override the default authorization. By default, any principal, like a user principal or service principal, within a Microsoft Entra tenant can create new management groups.

notes.front: Landing zone guidance says to keep the management group hierarchy reasonably flat, ideally with no more than {{c1::three to four}} levels.
notes.explanation: Fewer levels mean less management overhead and complexity.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Keep the management group hierarchy reasonably flat, ideally with no more than three to four levels. This restriction reduces management overhead and complexity.

notes.front: In the landing zone guidance, are management groups meant mainly for policy assignment or for billing and RBAC?
notes.back: For policy assignment.
notes.explanation: The guidance also warns against copying your organisation chart into a deeply nested hierarchy.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Don't duplicate your organizational structure into a deeply nested management group hierarchy. Use management groups for policy assignment versus billing and RBAC purposes.

notes.front: An application team asks for Contributor on the management group that holds its subscription. What does the landing zone guidance say?
notes.back: Don't grant it there; assign permissions at the individual subscription or resource group scopes the team needs.
notes.explanation: Assigning at management group scope brings over-permissioning, security risk and extra risk from inheritance.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Don't assign application teams permissions via RBAC at management group scopes. Instead, assign permissions at the individual subscription or resource group scopes that they require access to. This is normally handled during the subscription vending process. This is not recommended because of over-permissioning and security risks, and added risk from inheritance.

notes.front: A platform team needs access to every subscription for daily tasks and troubleshooting. How does the landing zone guidance suggest granting it?
notes.back: Through RBAC at management group scope, controlled by PIM so the permissions are granted only when needed.
notes.choices:
A) Management group scope RBAC, controlled through PIM
B) Permanent Owner at the root management group
C) A new management group for each platform engineer
notes.choicesExplained: B: a permanent assignment at the root reaches the whole directory and is never time-limited. C: management groups are for policy assignment, and extra groups add complexity without limiting access.
notes.explanation: Management group scope gives easy access to all subscriptions, and PIM keeps it from being standing access.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: You might assign permissions via RBAC at management group scopes for platform teams to grant them access to all subscriptions easily to perform daily tasks and troubleshooting. However, this should be controlled via privileged identity management (PIM) to ensure that the permissions are only granted when needed.

notes.front: What is a sandbox management group for, in the landing zone guidance?
notes.back: Experimenting with resources straight away, isolated from development, test and production environments.
notes.explanation: It lets people try resources before they are moved to production.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Create a sandbox management group so that you can immediately experiment with resources before you move them to production environments. The sandbox provides isolation from your development, test, and production environments.

notes.front: Why limit the number of Azure Policy assignments at the root management group?
notes.back: It minimises the debugging of inherited policies in lower-level management groups.
notes.explanation: Everything assigned at the root is inherited everywhere beneath it.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Limit the number of Azure Policy assignments at the root management group scope. This limitation minimizes debugging inherited policies in lower-level management groups.

notes.front: Developers keep creating Visual Studio benefit subscriptions that land under the root. What does the landing zone guidance recommend?
notes.back: Configure a default, dedicated management group for new subscriptions, such as a sandbox group.
notes.explanation: The default group keeps new subscriptions from going under the root management group.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management group recommendations”
notes.evidence: Configure a default, dedicated management group for new subscriptions. This group ensures that no subscriptions go under the root management group. This group is especially important if users have Microsoft Developer Network (MSDN) or Visual Studio benefits and subscriptions. A good candidate for this type of management group is a sandbox management group.

notes.front: In the Azure landing zone hierarchy, what is the difference between the Corp and Online management groups?
notes.back: Corp holds workloads needing connectivity to the corporate network through the hub; Online holds workloads that may need direct internet access.
notes.explanation: Placing a workload's subscription in one or the other decides which policies it inherits.
notes.source: Management groups, Cloud Adoption Framework (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Management groups in the Azure landing zone architecture”
notes.evidence: This group is for workloads that might require direct internet inbound or outbound connectivity or for workloads that might not require a virtual network. | |**Corp**| The dedicated management group for corporate landing zones. This group is for workloads that require connectivity or hybrid connectivity with the corporate network via the hub in the connectivity subscription.

notes.front: What is the difference between a platform landing zone and an application landing zone?
notes.back: The platform landing zone is the central foundation of governance, security and shared resources; application landing zones are where workload teams run their workloads.
notes.explanation: Workloads in application landing zones operate within the guardrails set by the platform landing zone.
notes.source: What is an Azure landing zone? (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “What is an Azure landing zone?”
notes.evidence: Platform landing zone: The centralized foundation that establishes governance, security, and shared resources for all your Azure workloads. - Application (workload) landing zones: The environments where workload teams deploy and operate workload resources within the guardrails of the platform landing zone.

notes.front: A company with one Microsoft Entra tenant plans a separate platform landing zone for each of its five business units. What does the guidance say?
notes.back: Most organisations should have only one platform landing zone per Microsoft Entra tenant.
notes.choices:
A) Build one platform landing zone for the tenant
B) Build one platform landing zone per business unit
C) Skip the platform landing zone and build only application landing zones
notes.choicesExplained: B: the guidance is one platform landing zone per tenant for most organisations. C: every Azure landing zone starts with the platform landing zone.
notes.explanation: The platform landing zone is the organisation's single Azure foundation: it defines how resources are organised, governed and shared centrally.
notes.source: What is an Azure landing zone? (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Platform landing zone”
notes.evidence: The platform landing zone establishes your organization's Azure foundation. It defines how you organize your Azure resources, enforce governance, and provide shared capabilities centrally. Most organizations should have only one platform landing zone per Microsoft Entra tenant.

notes.front: A workload has development, test and production environments, and production has outgrown one subscription's limits. How many application landing zones does it get, and can production use more than one subscription?
notes.back: One application landing zone; each environment can consist of one or more subscriptions.
notes.choices:
A) One landing zone; production may span several subscriptions
B) Three landing zones, one per environment
C) One landing zone that must fit in one subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: a workload has a single application landing zone holding all its environments. C: an environment can use more than one subscription when limits require it.
notes.explanation: Subscriptions are split by workload needs, team ownership or subscription limits, all within the workload's single landing zone.
notes.source: What is an Azure landing zone? (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Application landing zone”
notes.evidence: Each workload has a single application landing zone. An application landing zone contains all the environments required to support that workload, such as development, test, and production. Each environment consists of one or more Azure subscriptions based on workload requirements, team ownership boundaries, or Azure subscription limits.

notes.front: A new workload needs direct inbound internet access. Where does the platform team place its subscription, and how does it get its governance policies?
notes.back: Under the Online management group, inheriting the Azure Policy assignments applied to the hierarchy.
notes.choices:
A) Online management group; policies are inherited
B) Corp management group; policies are copied in by hand
C) The root management group; no policies apply
notes.choicesExplained: B: Corp is for workloads connecting to the corporate network through the hub, and policies arrive by inheritance. C: application landing zones go under the landing zones management group, not the root.
notes.explanation: The platform team picks Online, Corp or Local for each application landing zone subscription based on the workload's needs.
notes.source: What is an Azure landing zone? (MicrosoftDocs cloud-adoption-framework), “Application landing zone”
notes.evidence: Based on the requirements of the workload, the platform team places each application landing zone subscription in either the Online, Internal ("Corp"), or Local management group under the "(Application) Landing zones" management group. Each subscription and its Azure resources inherit the governance and security policies from the Azure Policies applied to the management group hierarchy.

notes.front: At which scopes can you apply resource tags, and where can't you?
notes.back: On resources, resource groups and subscriptions, but not on management groups.
notes.explanation: Management groups are the one level of the hierarchy that cannot carry tags.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Tag usage and recommendations”
notes.evidence: You can apply tags to your Azure resources, resource groups, and subscriptions but not to management groups.

notes.front: You tag a resource group with CostCentre = 4410. Do the virtual machines inside it get that tag?
notes.back: No. Resources don't inherit tags from a resource group or subscription; use Azure Policy to apply them.
notes.choices:
A) No; use Azure Policy to apply the tag
B) Yes, tags always flow down to child resources
C) Only resources created after the tag was added
notes.choicesExplained: B: resource tags do not inherit, unlike locks and policy assignments. C: new resources do not inherit the tag either.
notes.explanation: Tag policies are the documented way to carry tags from a subscription or resource group down to its resources.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Inherit tags”
notes.evidence: Resources don't inherit the tags you apply to a resource group or a subscription. To apply tags from a subscription or resource group to the resources, see Assign policy definitions for tag compliance.

notes.front: Finance needs every new resource to carry a CostCentre tag even when engineers forget to add one. What should you assign?
notes.back: An Azure Policy with the modify effect, such as the built-in 'Add a tag to resources'.
notes.choices:
A) A policy with the modify effect that adds the tag
B) The tag on the subscription, so resources inherit it
C) A CanNotDelete lock on the subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: resources do not inherit tags from a subscription. C: a lock blocks deletion; it does not add tags.
notes.explanation: That policy adds a required tag and its default value when the deployment request does not specify it.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Policy definition”
notes.evidence: Add a tag to resources (Modify): Applies a required tag and its default value if the deploy request doesn't specify it.

notes.front: Each resource, resource group and subscription can have a maximum of {{c1::50}} tag name-value pairs.
notes.explanation: If you need more, a single tag value can hold a structured string with many values.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Limitations”
notes.evidence: Each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs. If you need to apply more tags than the maximum allowed number, use a JSON string for the tag value.

notes.front: Why must you never put sensitive values in resource tags?
notes.back: Tags are stored as plain text, so values can be exposed, for example through cost reports and exported templates.
notes.explanation: The documentation lists other exposures too, such as deployment histories and monitoring logs.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Tag usage and recommendations”
notes.evidence: Tags are stored as plain text. Do not add sensitive values to tags. Sensitive values could be exposed through many methods, including cost reports, commands that return existing tag definitions, deployment histories, exported templates, and monitoring logs.

notes.front: According to Cost Management, what is the only way to add your own business context to cost details?
notes.back: Resource tags.
notes.explanation: Tags are perhaps the most flexible way to map resources to applications, business units, environments and owners.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Cost Management (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Organize and allocate costs”
notes.evidence: Resource tags are the only way to add your own business context to cost details and are perhaps the most flexible way to map resources to applications, business units, environments, owners, etc.

notes.front: Several departments share one subscription, and finance wants each department's virtual machine usage shown separately on the bill. What should you do?
notes.back: Tag the resources with each department's cost centre and group the billing data by that tag.
notes.choices:
A) Tag resources by cost centre and group billing data by tag
B) Create a management group per department inside the subscription
C) Put a ReadOnly lock on each department's resources
notes.choicesExplained: B: management groups hold subscriptions, not resources inside one subscription. C: locks restrict changes and add nothing to billing data.
notes.explanation: Tags can group usage in billing data, for example by cost centre or by runtime environment.
notes.source: Use tags to organize your Azure resources and management hierarchy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Tags and billing”
notes.evidence: Use tags to group your billing data. For example, if you're running multiple virtual machines for different organizations, use the tags to group usage by cost center. You can also use tags to categorize costs by runtime environment, including the billing usage for virtual machines running in the production environment.

notes.front: What are the two kinds of resource lock called in the Azure portal, and what are they called on the command line?
notes.back: In the portal: Delete and Read-only. On the command line: CanNotDelete and ReadOnly.
notes.explanation: One kind prevents deletions; the other prevents modifications as well.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: You can set locks that prevent either deletions or modifications. In the portal, these locks are called **Delete** and **Read-only**. In the command line, these locks are called **CanNotDelete** and **ReadOnly**.

notes.front: What can authorised users still do to a resource that has a CanNotDelete lock?
notes.back: Read it and modify it, but not delete it.
notes.explanation: The lock blocks deletion only, so normal changes carry on.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it.

notes.front: Applying a ReadOnly lock is similar to restricting all authorised users to the permissions of which built-in role?
notes.back: The Reader role: they can read the resource but can't update or delete it.
notes.explanation: A ReadOnly lock stops both updates and deletions.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: ReadOnly means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it. Applying this lock is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the Reader role provides.

notes.front: How does a resource lock differ from Azure RBAC in whom it restricts?
notes.back: A lock applies its restriction across all users and roles; RBAC sets permissions for particular users and roles.
notes.explanation: Even an Owner is stopped by a lock until the lock is removed.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: Unlike with role-based access control (RBAC), you use management locks to apply a restriction across all users and roles.

notes.front: Nobody, whatever their role, should be able to delete a production database by accident, but day-to-day changes must continue. What do you apply?
notes.back: A CanNotDelete (Delete) lock on the database.
notes.choices:
A) A CanNotDelete lock
B) A ReadOnly lock
C) Removing the Owner role from administrators
notes.choicesExplained: B: ReadOnly also blocks the day-to-day changes. C: RBAC changes only affect the users you change, while a lock applies to everyone.
notes.explanation: A lock restricts all users and roles, and CanNotDelete still allows reads and modifications.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure”
notes.evidence: CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. - ReadOnly means authorized users can read a resource, but they can't delete or update it.

notes.front: You put a lock on a resource group. Do resources added to the group later also get it?
notes.back: Yes. All resources in the scope inherit the lock, including ones added later.
notes.explanation: Where locks stack, the most restrictive one in the inheritance chain takes precedence.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock inheritance”
notes.evidence: When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock. Even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. The most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.

notes.front: One virtual machine has a Delete lock. You try to delete its resource group, where nothing else is locked. What happens?
notes.back: The whole delete operation is blocked; nothing in the group is deleted.
notes.choices:
A) The whole deletion is blocked
B) Everything except the locked machine is deleted
C) Everything is deleted, because the group itself was not locked
notes.choicesExplained: B: partial deletion is not possible. C: a lock on any resource in the group blocks deletion of the group.
notes.explanation: A partial deletion isn't possible, even when the group and the other resources are unlocked.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Lock inheritance”
notes.evidence: If you have a Delete lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the feature blocks the whole delete operation. Even if the resource group or other resources in the resource group are unlocked, the deletion doesn't happen. A partial deletion isn't possible.

notes.front: Do resource locks restrict data plane operations?
notes.back: No. Locks apply only to control plane operations, which go to `management.azure.com`.
notes.explanation: Locks protect a resource from changes but don't restrict how it performs its functions.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Understand scope of locks”
notes.evidence: Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. Azure control plane operations go to `https://management.azure.com`.

notes.front: An administrator puts a CanNotDelete lock on a storage account of scanned invoices and says the invoices are now safe from deletion. Is that right?
notes.back: No. A lock on a storage account doesn't protect its data from being deleted or modified.
notes.explanation: Deleting a blob is a data plane operation, which locks do not cover.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Considerations before applying your locks”
notes.evidence: A read-only lock or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect its data from being deleted or modified. It also doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file.

notes.front: Which built-in roles have the access needed to create or delete resource locks?
notes.back: Owner and User Access Administrator.
notes.explanation: Locks need the `Microsoft.Authorization/*` or `Microsoft.Authorization/locks/*` actions; some specialised roles or a custom role can also grant them.
notes.source: Lock your Azure resources to protect your infrastructure (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Who can create or delete locks”
notes.evidence: To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions. Users assigned to the Owner and the User Access Administrator roles have the required access. Some specialized built-in roles also grant this access. You can create a custom role with the required permissions.

notes.front: What are two events that cause Azure Policy to evaluate a resource?
notes.back: For example, a resource is created or updated in a scope with a policy assignment, or that scope gets a new policy or initiative assignment.
notes.explanation: Updating an assigned policy and the standard evaluation cycle every 24 hours also trigger evaluation.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Understand evaluation outcomes”
notes.evidence: A resource is created or updated in a scope with a policy assignment. - A scope gets a new assignment of a policy or initiative. - A policy or initiative already assigned to a scope is updated. - The standard compliance evaluation cycle that occurs once every 24 hours.

notes.front: A governance engineer must create and manage Azure Policy definitions and assignments, but shouldn't be given full Owner rights. Which built-in role fits?
notes.back: Resource Policy Contributor.
notes.choices:
A) Resource Policy Contributor
B) Contributor
C) Reader
notes.choicesExplained: B: Contributor can trigger remediation but can't create or update definitions and assignments. C: Reader has only read access to policy operations.
notes.explanation: Resource Policy Contributor includes most Azure Policy operations. Contributor and Reader can read policy operations, and Contributor can trigger remediation, but neither can create or update definitions and assignments.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure RBAC permissions in Azure Policy”
notes.evidence: The Resource Policy Contributor role includes most Azure Policy operations. Owner has full rights. Both Contributor and Reader have access to all read Azure Policy operations.

notes.front: How many effects does a policy definition have, and what does the effect decide?
notes.back: One; it decides what happens when the policy rule matches.
notes.explanation: The effect sits in the policy rule, and it can behave differently for new, updated and existing resources.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Policy definitions effect basics”
notes.evidence: Each policy definition in Azure Policy has a single `effect` in its `policyRule`. That `effect` determines what happens when the policy rule is evaluated to match. The effects behave differently if they are for a new resource, an updated resource, or an existing resource.

notes.front: Which policy effect does the built-in Allowed Locations policy use to stop resources being created outside permitted regions?
notes.back: deny.
notes.explanation: The deny effect enforces geo-compliance by refusing new resources in locations not on the list.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Policy definition”
notes.evidence: Allowed Locations (Deny): Restricts the available locations for new resources. Its effect is used to enforce your geo-compliance requirements.

notes.front: What is the difference between what an audit policy and an auditIfNotExists policy look at?
notes.back: audit judges a resource by its own properties; auditIfNotExists judges it by a child or extension resource's properties.
notes.explanation: auditIfNotExists definitions also need extra details in the policy rule that audit ones do not.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Interchanging effects”
notes.evidence: audit policies assess a resource's compliance based on its own properties, while auditIfNotExists policies assess a resource's compliance based on a child or extension resource's properties.

notes.front: Which policy effect is checked first during evaluation, to decide whether the rule should be evaluated at all?
notes.back: disabled.
notes.explanation: The effect is also interchangeable with any other effect.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Order of evaluation”
notes.evidence: disabled is checked first to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated.

notes.front: Which two effects are evaluated before deny and audit because they could alter the request?
notes.back: append and modify.
notes.explanation: A change they make might stop an audit or deny effect from triggering; both work only in Resource Manager mode.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Order of evaluation”
notes.evidence: append and modify are then evaluated. Since either could alter the request, a change made might prevent an audit or deny effect from triggering. These effects are only available with a Resource Manager mode.

notes.front: Which policy effect lets Azure Policy block certain actions on resources?
notes.back: denyAction.
notes.explanation: This is one way Azure Policy acts on actions and not only on resource properties.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC”
notes.evidence: Azure Policy through DenyAction effect can also block certain actions on resources.

notes.front: Which two effects evaluate only after the resource provider has returned success, to decide whether more logging or action is needed?
notes.back: auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists.
notes.explanation: The two effects are often interchangeable.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Order of evaluation”
notes.evidence: After the Resource Provider returns a success code on a Resource Manager mode request, auditIfNotExists and deployIfNotExists evaluate to determine whether more compliance logging or action is required.

notes.front: Several policy assignments at different scopes affect one resource. How is the combined result described?
notes.back: Cumulative most restrictive: each assignment is evaluated on its own.
notes.explanation: Because every assignment is evaluated individually, a resource can't slip through a gap between scopes.
notes.source: Azure Policy definitions effect basics (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Layering policy definitions”
notes.evidence: Each assignment is individually evaluated. As such, there isn't an opportunity for a resource to slip through a gap from differences in scope. The net result of layering policy definitions is considered to be **cumulative most restrictive**.

notes.front: When you introduce a new policy, which effects should you start with instead of deny, modify or deployIfNotExists?
notes.back: audit or auditIfNotExists.
notes.explanation: They let you track how the definition affects your resources; an enforcement effect might hinder automation already in place, such as autoscale scripts.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Recommendations for managing policies”
notes.evidence: Start with an `audit` or `auditIfNotExists` effect instead of an enforcement (`deny`, `modify`, `deployIfNotExists`) effect to track how your policy definition affects the resources in your environment. If you have scripts already in place to autoscale your applications, setting an enforcement effect might hinder such automation tasks already in place.

notes.front: You want every virtual machine in a busy production subscription to have a backup tag, but scripts there create machines automatically and you don't know how many would fail. What is the safest first step?
notes.back: Assign the policy with the audit effect and review which resources would be non-compliant.
notes.choices:
A) Assign it with the audit effect first
B) Assign it with the deny effect immediately
C) Put a ReadOnly lock on the subscription
notes.choicesExplained: B: deny could block the scripts' deployments before you know the impact. C: a lock would stop the automation entirely and does nothing for tags.
notes.explanation: Starting with audit shows the impact, while an enforcement effect might break the automation already in place.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Recommendations for managing policies”
notes.evidence: Start with an `audit` or `auditIfNotExists` effect instead of an enforcement (`deny`, `modify`, `deployIfNotExists`) effect to track how your policy definition affects the resources in your environment. If you have scripts already in place to autoscale your applications, setting an enforcement effect might hinder such automation tasks already in place.

notes.front: Where does Microsoft recommend creating policy definitions, and where should you then create the assignments?
notes.back: Create definitions high, at management group or subscription level; create assignments at the next child level.
notes.explanation: A definition created at a management group can be assigned to a subscription or resource group within it.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Recommendations for managing policies”
notes.evidence: We recommend creating definitions at higher levels such as the management group or subscription level. Then, create the assignment at the next child level. If you create a definition at a management group, the assignment can be scoped down to a subscription or resource group within that management group.

notes.front: You are rolling out one security policy now and expect several related ones next quarter. How should you package it?
notes.back: Create and assign an initiative definition containing the single policy.
notes.choices:
A) An initiative holding the one policy
B) A separate assignment for each policy as it arrives
C) A management group for each policy
notes.choicesExplained: B: this grows the number of assignments to manage with every new policy. C: management groups organise subscriptions; they are not a way to package policies.
notes.explanation: Policies added to the initiative later join the existing assignment, so the number of assignments to manage doesn't grow.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Recommendations for managing policies”
notes.evidence: We recommend creating and assigning initiative definitions even if starting with a single policy definition. This method enables you to add policy definitions to the initiative later without increasing the number of assignments to manage.

notes.front: A deny policy assigned at a management group blocks networking resources. One child subscription legitimately needs them. What do you do?
notes.back: Exclude that subscription from the management group assignment, then assign a more permissive policy on it if needed.
notes.choices:
A) Exclude the subscription from the parent assignment
B) Assign a more permissive policy on the subscription only
C) Give the subscription's team the Owner role
notes.choicesExplained: B: the parent's deny still applies, because a permissive child assignment cannot override it. C: Azure Policy blocks non-compliant resources whatever the user's role.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy is an explicit deny system, so a more permissive assignment lower down does not override the parent's deny.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Assignments”
notes.evidence: However, this example wouldn't work because Azure Policy is an explicit deny system. Instead, you need to exclude the child management group or subscription from the management group-level assignment. Then, assign the more permissive definition on the child management group or subscription level.

notes.front: A policy is assigned at management group level. Which resources does Azure Policy actually evaluate?
notes.back: Only resources at the subscription or resource group level.
notes.explanation: The assignment can sit at the management group, but evaluation happens on the resources beneath it.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Resources covered by Azure Policy”
notes.evidence: Although a policy can be assigned at the management group level, only resources at the subscription or resource group level are evaluated.

notes.front: What does Azure Policy focus on, compared with Azure RBAC?
notes.back: Azure Policy checks that resource state complies with business rules, whoever made the change; Azure RBAC manages what users can do.
notes.explanation: The two work together: RBAC controls actions by user, and Azure Policy controls the resulting state.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC”
notes.evidence: Azure Policy ensures that resource state is compliant to your business rules without concern for who made the change or who has permission to make a change.

notes.front: A user holds Contributor on a subscription and tries to create a virtual machine in a region that an assigned deny policy forbids. What happens?
notes.back: Azure Policy blocks the creation, even though the user's role allows the action.
notes.choices:
A) The deny policy blocks it
B) It succeeds, because Contributor allows creating resources
C) It succeeds but is logged as non-compliant
notes.choicesExplained: B: RBAC permission does not override Azure Policy. C: that would be an audit effect; this assignment uses deny.
notes.explanation: Having access to perform an action does not stop Azure Policy blocking a create or update whose result is non-compliant.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Policy and Azure RBAC”
notes.evidence: Azure RBAC focuses on managing user actions at different scopes. If control of an action is required based on user information, then Azure RBAC is the correct tool to use. Even if an individual has access to perform an action, if the result is a non-compliant resource, Azure Policy still blocks the create or update.

notes.front: After you assign a new policy, 300 existing resources show as non-compliant. How does Azure Policy help bring them into line without redeploying each one?
notes.back: Through remediation: bulk remediation for existing resources.
notes.choices:
A) Run a remediation for the existing resources
B) Delete and recreate each resource
C) Change the effect to disabled
notes.choicesExplained: B: remediation exists so that you do not have to redeploy. C: disabling the policy stops evaluation; it fixes nothing.
notes.explanation: Azure Policy offers bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new ones.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Policy?”
notes.evidence: It also helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources.

notes.front: What does the managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment need?
notes.back: Enough permissions to create or update the resources it targets.
notes.explanation: Granting those permissions to the managed identity needs the User Access Administrator role.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Policy (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure RBAC permissions in Azure Policy”
notes.evidence: The managed identity of a deployIfNotExists or modify policy assignment needs enough permissions to create or update targeted resources.

notes.front: Azure Blueprints (Preview) is being retired on {{c1::31 January 2027}}, with a phased retirement beginning on 31 July 2026.
notes.explanation: Blueprint definitions and assignments should be migrated before the retirement date.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Blueprints (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Blueprints retirement”
notes.evidence: Azure Blueprints (Preview) is being retired on **January 31, 2027**, with a phased retirement beginning July 31, 2026.

notes.front: A team plans to use Azure Blueprints for repeatable, governed environments starting in 2027. What should they use instead?
notes.back: Azure Deployment Stacks (recommended) and template specs.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Deployment Stacks and template specs
B) Azure Blueprints, since it is still in preview
C) Azure Resource Graph
notes.choicesExplained: B: Blueprints is being retired and will not be available. C: Resource Graph queries resources; it does not deploy environments.
notes.explanation: Blueprints retire on 31 January 2027, and the documentation directs migrations to deployment stacks and template specs.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Blueprints (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “Azure Blueprints retirement”
notes.evidence: Migrate your blueprint definitions and assignments to Azure Deployment Stacks (recommended) and template specs before the retirement date.

notes.front: Before assigning a new policy across hundreds of subscriptions, you want to see which resources it would affect. Which service helps you query that at scale?
notes.back: Azure Resource Graph.
notes.choices:
A) Azure Resource Graph
B) Microsoft Cost Management
C) Resource locks
notes.choicesExplained: B: Cost Management analyses spending, not resource properties. C: locks restrict changes; they do not query anything.
notes.explanation: Its queries can assess the effect of applying policies in a large cloud environment.
notes.source: Overview of Azure Resource Graph (MicrosoftDocs azure-docs), “What is Azure Resource Graph?”
notes.evidence: Explore resources iteratively based on governance requirements. - Assess the effect of applying policies in a vast cloud environment.

notes.front: Which cloud security posture management capabilities come free with Defender for Cloud, and how do you get the advanced ones?
notes.back: Foundational CSPM is free; the advanced capabilities need the paid Defender CSPM plan.
notes.explanation: Foundational CSPM covers basics such as the secure score, while tools like attack path analysis need the paid plan.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “Cloud security posture management (CSPM)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A security lead wants one figure that summarises the organisation's cloud security posture and goes up as teams fix Defender for Cloud recommendations. What should they track?
notes.back: The secure score.
notes.choices:
A) The secure score
B) The Azure Policy compliance count
C) The monthly Cost Management budget
notes.choicesExplained: B: policy compliance counts non-compliant resources per policy; it is not Defender's posture summary. C: budgets track spending, not security.
notes.explanation: The secure score is a free posture capability that rises as recommendations are remediated.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “Cloud security posture management (CSPM)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the difference between CSPM and CWPP in Defender for Cloud?
notes.back: CSPM checks and improves how securely resources are configured; CWPP defends running workloads against threats.
notes.explanation: One looks at set-up and recommendations, the other at detecting and responding to attacks on workloads.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: You must detect threats against Windows and Linux machines running in Azure and in your own datacentre. Which Defender for Cloud plan fits?
notes.back: Defender for Servers.
notes.choices:
A) Defender for Servers
B) Defender CSPM
C) Defender for Storage
notes.choicesExplained: B: Defender CSPM improves posture; threat detection on machines is a workload protection plan. C: Defender for Storage protects storage accounts, not machines.
notes.explanation: It provides threat detection and advanced defences for Windows and Linux machines in Azure, other clouds and on-premises.
notes.source: What is Microsoft Defender for Cloud? (Microsoft Learn), “Cloud workload protection platform (CWPP)”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the regulatory compliance dashboard show for each enabled standard?
notes.back: The standard's controls and the security assessments for them, whose status reflects your compliance.
notes.explanation: It helps you focus on the gaps in a standard and follow compliance over time.
notes.source: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Microsoft Learn), “Assess regulatory compliance”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which compliance standard is turned on by default when you enable Defender for Cloud on an Azure subscription?
notes.back: The Microsoft cloud security benchmark.
notes.explanation: Other standards can be added on top of this default one.
notes.source: Improve regulatory compliance in Microsoft Defender for Cloud (Microsoft Learn), “Before you start”

notes.front: Auditors want your status against a standard that is not enabled by default, and you run only the free Defender for Cloud features. What must you do before adding it to the dashboard?

B) Assign the Security Reader role to the auditors
C) Nothing; any standard can be added on the free tier

notes.back: Use Download report on the regulatory compliance dashboard.
